title: Question 9
stem: Fluorine-18 ($^{18}_{9}\text{F}$) decays by beta-plus ($\beta^{+}$) emission with a half-life of 110 minutes.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State the name of the beta-plus particle.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the charge on the emitted particle when a proton in the nucleus changes to a neutron, and what particle has the same mass as an electron but opposite charge.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall What Beta-Plus Means**
In a proton-rich nucleus like $^{18}_{9}\text{F}$, a proton converts to a neutron and emits a particle with charge $+e$ and essentially the same mass as an electron. This antimatter electron is called a positron.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the decay constant of fluorine-18 is $1.05 \times 10^{-4}\text{s}^{-1}$.
hints: Hint 1: Remember how $\lambda$ is linked to half-life $T_{1/2}$ by $\ln 2$, and check that $T_{1/2}$ must be in seconds, so convert 110 minutes first.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Half-Life to Decay Constant**
For any radioactive nuclide, a larger decay constant means faster decay. They are linked by $$\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$$ where $T_{1/2}$ must be in seconds because $\lambda$ is in $\text{s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Convert and Calculate**
Convert the half-life: $$T_{1/2} = 110 \times 60 = 6600\text{ s}$$ Then $$\lambda = \frac{0.693}{6600} = 1.05 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}^{-1}$$ as required.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Determine the activity of $2.1 \times 10^{-12}\text{kg}$ of fluorine-18.
hints: Hint 1: Activity depends on how many unstable nuclei $N$ you have, so start by thinking how to get $N$ from the tiny mass and the nucleon number 18.
Hint 2: Recall that one nucleus of $^{18}$F has mass about $18u$ where $u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and that activity is linked to $N$ by $A = \lambda N$.
Hint 3: Calculate $N$ first, then multiply by $\lambda = 1.05 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}^{-1}$ from (a)(ii) and give the answer in $\text{Bq}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Number of Nuclei N**
You have mass, not count. Each fluorine-18 nucleus contains 18 nucleons, so its mass is about $18u$. With $u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$: $$N = \frac{M}{18u} = \frac{2.1 \times 10^{-12}}{18 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}}$$ This gives $$N \approx 7.0 \times 10^{13} \text{ nuclei}$$ Even a picogram contains a huge number of atoms.

Step 2: **Use Activity Law**
Activity is the decay rate: $$A = \lambda N$$ It tells you how many decays per second, with unit becquerel where $1\text{ Bq} = 1\text{ s}^{-1}$.

Step 3: **Calculate Activity**
Insert $\lambda = 1.05 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}^{-1}$: $$A = (1.05 \times 10^{-4}) \times (7.0 \times 10^{13}) \approx 7.4 \times 10^{9}\text{ Bq}$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: A small sample of fluorine-18 injected into the body acts as a tracer for use in medical imaging.
parts.text: Describe how the interaction of a $\beta^{+}$ particle with an electron in the body enables the formation of an image.

markscheme_points.text: (pair) annihilation occurs; the mass of the two particles is converted into energy; two gamma photons are formed and travel in opposite directions or two gamma photons are formed and leave the body; difference in arrival times of photons (at detector) is processed; Any three points, 1 mark each

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens when matter meets its exact antimatter partner inside the tissue.
Hint 2: Remember Einstein mass-energy equivalence and what type of highly penetrating photon is produced when mass disappears.
Hint 3: Consider why two photons emitted back-to-back are so useful for locating exactly where the decay happened using detectors around the body.
parts.proper_answer: The positron meets an electron and pair annihilation occurs. Mass is converted to energy as two gamma photons emitted in opposite directions. External detectors detect the photons in coincidence and the difference in arrival times locates the emission point to build an image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Annihilation in Tissue**
The emitted positron travels only a very short distance before meeting an ordinary electron in the body. Particle and antiparticle annihilate each other. Their total mass disappears and is converted into electromagnetic energy, conserving both energy ($E = mc^2$) and momentum.

Step 2: **Two Back-to-Back Gamma Photons**
To conserve momentum, annihilation produces two gamma-ray photons of equal energy travelling in exactly opposite directions away from the point of decay. These gamma rays are highly penetrating and easily leave the body.

Step 3: **Detection to Form Image**
A ring of detectors around the patient detects the two photons almost simultaneously (coincidence detection). The line joining the two detection points must pass through the decay point, and small differences in arrival time help pinpoint position. A computer processes many such events to map where tracer has concentrated, forming the image.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest why 110 minutes is a suitable half-life for a nuclide used as a tracer in medical diagnosis.

markscheme_points.text: with a shorter half-life: sample would (almost) fully decay before the test is complete
a longer half-life: exposes patient to harmful/ionising radiation unnecessarily or with a longer half-life: a larger dose (of tracer) needed to produce detectable activity

hints: Hint 1: Imagine what would go wrong if the half-life were only a few seconds compared with the time needed to prepare the tracer and complete a scan.
Hint 2: Imagine the opposite extreme of a half-life of many years and what that means for how long the patient stays radioactive and how much tracer you would need.
parts.proper_answer: If half-life much shorter, activity would decay away before imaging is complete. If half-life much longer, patient remains radioactive for a long time giving unnecessary dose, or a larger mass of tracer would be needed to give sufficient activity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Not Much Shorter**
A tracer must stay active long enough to be made, injected, circulate, and be scanned. With a much shorter half-life the sample would almost fully decay before the test is complete, so no useful signal remains.

Step 2: **Why Not Much Longer**
With a much longer half-life, the decay rate $A = \lambda N$ is very low, so you would need a larger dose to get a detectable count rate. Also the nuclide would continue irradiating the patient long after the scan, giving harmful ionising radiation exposure with no medical benefit. 110 minutes is a good compromise: high enough activity for imaging but decays away quickly afterwards.
